prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Assess the competitive advantages (economic moat) and pricing power of the publicly listed company "Duke Energy CORP" (ticker DUK), and list its competitors. Use the most recent information you know. Never invent figures: use null when unsure. Be specific (products, numbers, years).

Reply with ONLY one JSON object, no other text, in exactly this shape:
{
 "name": "official company name", "ticker": "DUK", "industry": "industry in a few words",
 "markets": ["the main product markets it competes in"],
 "mission": {"statement": "the company's own official mission statement, word for word as it publishes it; null if you are not sure of the exact wording (never paraphrase here)",
             "source": "where it is published, e.g. company website or 2025 annual report, or null",
             "plain": "what the mission means, in one short simple sentence"},
 "about": {"plain": "3-4 short sentences explaining what the company does, in simple everyday words a 12-year-old would understand; no jargon",
           "customers": "who buys from it, in one simple sentence",
           "everyday": "one sentence linking it to something ordinary people know or use, or null",
           "money": [ {"part": "business line in simple words", "share": decimal share of sales or null, "plain": "what it sells there, in a few simple words", "tag": "main|new|moonshot"} ]  (its main ways of making money, largest first, up to 6; also include any new business line or one with explosive, moonshot potential even if its sales are still small. tag: "main" = an established line that brings in a large part of sales; "new" = launched or entered in roughly the last 3 years; "moonshot" = could grow many times over or reshape the company, e.g. a new technology or market, even if unproven. Give each line one tag, the one that fits best)},
 "summary": "2-3 plain-English sentences on whether and why it has a competitive advantage",
 "pricingPower": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "specific evidence, e.g. price rises and what happened to volumes"},
 "moats": [ {"source": one of ["Brand and intangible assets","Switching costs","Network effects","Cost advantage and scale","Efficient scale","Counter-positioning","Process power (hard-to-copy know-how)","Cornered resource (exclusive asset or talent)"], "strength": "strong|moderate|weak|none", "evidence": "one or two specific sentences"} ]  (all 8 sources, in that order),
 "customers": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "customer satisfaction and loyalty: retention, NPS, reviews, repeat purchase"},
 "talent": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "ability to attract and keep top talent: employer rankings, reputation, pay"},
 "product": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "is the product best in class? independent benchmarks, awards, ecosystem"},
 "competitors": [ {"name": "company name", "ticker": "main listing ticker (exchange suffix if not US, e.g. 005930.KS) or null if private",
                   "usTicker": "ticker of its US listing or ADR that files reports with the SEC, or null", "overlap": "high|medium|low",
                   "note": "where they compete"} ]  (every significant competitor, most direct first, up to 15; include major private ones with ticker null),
 "estimates": [ {"name": "company name", "fy": "FY2025", "currency": "USD", "revenueUSDm": number, "revenueGrowth3y": decimal, "grossMargin": decimal, "operatingMargin": decimal, "netMargin": decimal} ]
   (approximate latest fiscal-year figures for the company itself and for every listed competitor; decimals, e.g. 0.42; null if unknown),
 "marketShare": [ {"market": "market name", "measure": "revenue|units|shipments|...", "latestYear": "2025", "earlierYear": "2020",
                   "rows": [ {"name": "company name", "latest": decimal or null, "earlier": decimal or null} ] } ]  (up to 3 of its main markets, the company and its main rivals),
 "threats": ["specific things that could weaken its advantage"],
 "ceo": {"name": "current CEO", "founder": true or false, "since": "YYYY", "background": "e.g. electrical engineer, Stanford MBA"},
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence with names, numbers or examples"} }  for EVERY id below:
   "c1": Rule Breaker #1: is it the leader of an important industry that is still emerging and growing fast?
   "c2": Rule Breaker #2: why do customers choose it over rivals (brand, better value, innovation, culture, leadership), and is that advantage hard to copy and likely to last many years?
   "c3": Rule Breaker #5: do ordinary people recognise the name, is it the default leader in its field (like Google, Amazon, NVIDIA, Tesla, Intuitive Surgical, Netflix), and would customers recommend its product?
   "c4": Does it have an inspiring mission it keeps emphasising, with management driven by purpose rather than money? If it spends 10 years doing this, would it matter?
   "c6": What is the general public consensus about the company and its products or services? When people hear the name, what are the first few descriptive words that come to mind? Start the evidence with those words in quotes (e.g. “innovative, premium, reliable”), then say whether that impression is mostly positive.
   "c7": Is its total addressable market large and growing, riding a secular trend (like CRWD, NVDA, TSLA, AMZN)?
   "c8": Does it have room to expand into big new markets: in its name, its technology or its vision?
   "m1": Is the CEO a visionary with a clear picture of the future?
   "m2": Is the CEO a founder (or acting like one): long-term thinking, working extraordinarily hard, pouring heart and soul into building something that outlives them?
   "m4": Does the CEO lead by serving employees and customers?
   "m5": Has the CEO deliberately built a strong, distinctive culture that keeps inventing new products and technologies?
   "m6": Is the CEO deeply hands-on with the product and technology, ideally with an engineering background?
   "m7": Is the CEO a person of great character who cares about something bigger than profit? For successor CEOs: is stewardship aimed at the benefit of humanity?
   "m7b": Has the CEO been invited to give a commencement speech at a top university (Stanford, Harvard, MIT, etc.)? Name it.
   "m8b": Does the CEO have a distinctive, memorable personality (like Elon Musk, Alex Karp, Larry Page)?
   "m9": Has the CEO a strong record of execution and results?
   "m10": Is the CEO and company known for frugality (like Bezos's door desk)?
   "c10": Do its products solve problems for people all over the world, greatly improving the lives of a very large number of people (like NFLX, GOOG, ISRG)?
   "p2": Is what it builds extremely hard to do, and important to the world?
   "f1": Has revenue grown in almost every one of the last five years?
   "f2": Have gross and operating margins risen over the last five years?
   "f3": Is debt low compared with cash and cash flow, with positive shareholders' equity?
   "f4": Have operating income and operating cash flow risen over the last five years?
   "v1": Is its main product clearly the best in its field, with a practical reason an ordinary person can understand for choosing it over every alternative (like NVIDIA over AMD)?
   "v2": Is it widely seen as one of the best companies to work for (culture, mission, reputation, employer rankings)? Cite rankings.
   "c5": Do its products make the world better? If it disappeared overnight, who would notice and miss it, and why?
 "asOf": "YYYY-MM of the newest information you used"
}

result.name: Duke Energy Corporation
result.industry: Regulated electric and natural gas utility
markets: Regulated retail electricity in North Carolina, South Carolina, Florida, Indiana, Ohio and Kentucky
Regulated natural gas distribution in North Carolina, South Carolina, Ohio and Kentucky
Power supply for data centers and other large industrial loads
Wholesale electricity sales to cooperatives and municipalities

mission.statement: Our purpose at Duke Energy is to power the lives of our customers and the vitality of our communities.
mission.source: Duke Energy purpose statement as published on its 3BL Media corporate campaign page
mission.plain: Keep the lights on and the gas flowing so people and their towns can thrive.

about.plain: Duke Energy makes electricity and sends it through wires to homes and businesses in six states, mostly in the Southeast and Midwest. It also pipes natural gas to homes for heating and cooking. It owns big power plants, including nuclear, gas, coal, water and solar plants. Because it is usually the only power company allowed in its areas, state officials decide what it can charge.
about.customers: About 8.7 million electric and 1.6 million natural gas customers: families, shops, factories and, increasingly, giant data centers.
about.everyday: When someone in Charlotte, Orlando or Indianapolis turns on a light or charges a phone, the electricity very likely comes from Duke Energy.

money.plain: electricity for homes, businesses and factories in six states
natural gas piped to homes and businesses
long-term contracts to power huge computer centers

money.part: New nuclear (large reactors or small modular reactors)
money.plain: possible next generation of nuclear plants

result.summary: Duke has a durable, government-granted advantage: it is the exclusive electric utility in large, growing parts of the Carolinas, Florida, Indiana and Kentucky, so no rival can build a competing grid there. Regulators set its prices and returns, so the moat protects steady earnings rather than outsized profits; a $103B 2026-2030 capital plan and 7.8 GW of signed data-center contracts give it above-average growth for a utility.

pricingPower.evidence: Prices are set by state commissions: 2025 revenue rose 6.2% to $32,237M on rate increases in the Carolinas, Florida, Indiana and Kentucky while retail customers kept growing (+1.4% in Q2 2026), but allowed returns are capped (the 2026 Duke Energy Carolinas North Carolina settlement sets a 9.8% ROE) and affordability pressure forced measures such as tax-credit flow-back to offset a 2027 Florida base-rate increase.

moats.evidence: Its key intangible assets are exclusive state franchises and regulatory relationships rather than a consumer brand; Fortune ranked it No. 3 of 15 electric and gas utilities in its 2026 World's Most Admired Companies list.
Retail customers in North Carolina, South Carolina, Florida, Indiana and Kentucky cannot choose another electric supplier, and new data-center agreements include minimum-take provisions.
A customer gains nothing from more customers joining the grid.

With 55,700 MW of owned capacity, 8.7 million electric customers and $195.7B of assets, it can finance a $103B five-year capital plan and secure scarce gas turbines (access to 26 GE Vernova units) more easily than smaller utilities.
Its service territories support only one transmission and distribution network; duplicating the grid would be uneconomic, which is why states grant it a regulated monopoly.
It is an incumbent regulated utility, not a new business model incumbents cannot copy.
Decades of running one of the largest US nuclear fleets, including subsequent license renewals and planned uprates of about 300 MW, is know-how few utilities have.
Exclusive franchises in fast-growing Sun Belt states plus existing nuclear, hydro and transmission assets and sites that a newcomer could not replicate.

customers.evidence: Customers stay because they must, but satisfaction is middling: in J.D. Power's 2025 residential study Duke Energy Florida scored 527 (3rd of 12, equal to the South Large average), while Duke Energy Progress (516) and Duke Energy Carolinas (515, 9th of 12) were below average and the Midwest entry scored 504 (10th of 15).

talent.evidence: A stable, well-paying employer that Fortune has listed among the World's Most Admired Companies for nine consecutive years (No. 3 utility in 2026), but it does not appear on top-tier best-places-to-work lists dominated by tech firms.

product.evidence: Electricity is a commodity; Duke's distinction is a large, diverse fleet (55,700 MW including nuclear, gas, hydro and solar) and reliability, but customers judge mainly on price and outages, and its J.D. Power scores are mostly at or below peer averages.

competitors.name: The Southern Company
competitors.note: Neighboring Southeast regulated utility; competes for data-center and industrial sitings and investor capital.

competitors.name: NextEra Energy, Inc.
competitors.note: Florida Power & Light borders Duke Energy Florida; competes for large loads, renewables and capital.

competitors.name: Dominion Energy, Inc.
competitors.note: Dominion Energy South Carolina and Virginia operations neighbor Duke's Carolinas utilities and compete for data-center load; being acquired by NextEra.

competitors.name: American Electric Power Company, Inc.
competitors.note: Neighboring regulated utility in Ohio, Indiana and Kentucky competing for data centers and industrial sitings.

competitors.name: Tennessee Valley Authority
competitors.note: Federal power producer bordering the Carolinas and Kentucky; competes for large industrial and data-center sitings.

competitors.name: Santee Cooper (South Carolina Public Service Authority)
competitors.note: State-owned South Carolina utility competing for large industrial and data-center load.

competitors.name: North Carolina Electric Membership Corporation and NC electric cooperatives
competitors.note: Cooperatives serving rural North Carolina; compete for new loads at territory edges and buy wholesale power from Duke.

competitors.name: NiSource Inc.
competitors.note: NIPSCO electric and gas utility in northern Indiana competing for data-center and industrial sitings.

competitors.name: Emera Inc. (Tampa Electric)
competitors.note: Tampa Electric serves the Tampa area next to Duke Energy Florida.

competitors.name: Vistra Corp.
competitors.note: Competitive generator and retail supplier; competes for Ohio retail customers and data-center power deals.

competitors.name: Constellation Energy Corporation
competitors.note: Nuclear generator and retail supplier competing in Ohio retail choice and for clean-power deals with hyperscalers.

competitors.name: Spire Inc.
competitors.note: Gas utility peer; bought Duke's Piedmont Tennessee gas business in 2026.

competitors.name: Enbridge Inc. (Enbridge Gas North Carolina)
competitors.note: Gas distributor in North Carolina alongside Duke's Piedmont Natural Gas.

estimates.name: Santee Cooper (South Carolina Public Service Authority)
North Carolina Electric Membership Corporation and NC electric cooperatives

threats: Affordability backlash and regulatory pushback on rate increases as the $103B capital plan flows into bills
Allowed returns set by regulators (e.g. 9.8% ROE in the 2026 DEC North Carolina settlement) could be cut
Data-center demand may not materialize at the scale of the 15.4 GW late-stage pipeline, leaving stranded investment
Rising interest rates and heavy debt ($91.2B at June 30, 2026) raise financing costs and require ongoing equity issuance
Hurricanes and storms in Florida and the Carolinas causing large outage and recovery costs
Distributed generation (rooftop solar plus batteries) and large customers self-generating could erode sales
Cost overruns and first-of-a-kind risk if it commits to new nuclear (AP1000 or SMRs)

ceo.name: Harry Sideris
ceo.background: Chemical engineer (BS, NC State), MBA from Campbell University; joined Carolina Power & Light/Progress Energy in 1996 and rose through generation, Duke Energy Florida president and customer-experience roles

c1.evidence: Electric utilities are a mature, regulated industry; Duke is one of the largest US energy holding companies but the industry is not emerging, even with data-center demand (7.8 GW signed).

c2.evidence: Customers do not choose it: state-granted monopoly franchises in NC, SC, FL, IN and KY make it the only option, an advantage that is very hard to copy and long-lasting but not earned through product superiority.

c3.evidence: The name is well known across the Carolinas, Florida and the Midwest as the local power company, but customers rarely recommend it (J.D. Power 2025 scores mostly at or below segment averages).

c4.evidence: Its purpose is 'to power the lives of our customers and the vitality of our communities', which matters for millions of people, but management is driven mainly by regulated returns and 5-7% EPS growth targets.

c6.evidence: “utility, power bills, reliable, expensive” - the impression is mixed: people see it as dependable but resent rising bills and storm outages.

c7.evidence: Electricity demand is growing again on data centers, reshoring and Sun Belt population growth (late-stage pipeline of 15.4 GW), but its market is limited to its regulated territories.

c8.evidence: It can grow within its territories via data-center load, new gas generation (15 GW of new capacity planned by 2031) and possibly new nuclear, but regulation keeps it out of new geographic markets.

m1.evidence: Sideris has laid out a clear plan (15 GW of new capacity by 2031, nuclear life extensions to 80 years, evaluating AP1000/SMRs) but it is an operational plan rather than a bold vision.

m2.evidence: Sideris is a career executive who joined Carolina Power & Light in 1996 and became CEO on April 1, 2025; he is not a founder.

m4.evidence: He led Duke's customer experience organization before becoming president, and the company introduced a 'Customer Protection Plus' framework in July 2026 so large users pay their own costs.

m5.evidence: Duke's culture is a safety- and reliability-focused regulated utility culture, not one known for inventing new products and technologies.

m6.evidence: Sideris is a chemical engineer (NC State) who spent years running power plants in the Carolinas and Florida before moving into executive roles.

m7.evidence: No public controversies are known, and his stewardship focuses on reliable, affordable power, but there is little public evidence either way about his character beyond corporate statements.

m7b.evidence: No record was found of Harry Sideris giving a commencement speech at a top university.

m8b.evidence: Sideris keeps a low public profile typical of utility CEOs.

m9.evidence: In his first year as CEO Duke delivered 2025 EPS of $6.31 (above guidance midpoint), lifted Q2 2026 adjusted EPS to $1.43 from $1.25, and signed 7.8 GW of data-center agreements.

m10.evidence: Duke is not known for frugality; it is a capital-intensive utility whose earnings grow by investing more ($103B five-year plan).

c10.evidence: It powers the daily lives of about 8.7 million electric and 1.6 million gas customers, a very large number of people, but only in six US states.

p2.evidence: Running a 55,700 MW fleet including nuclear reactors and a grid across six states is technically demanding and essential.

f1.evidence: Revenue rose every year from $23,366M in 2020 to $24,621M, $28,768M, $29,060M, $30,357M and $32,237M in 2025 (10-K).

f2.evidence: Operating margin rose from 19.6% in 2020 to 26.8% in 2025 (dipping only in 2022, to 20.9%), and revenue less fuel and purchased power rose from 74.1% to 75.0% of revenue.

f3.evidence: Debt is very high: $91,238M (short-term plus long-term) against only $673M cash at June 30, 2026 and 2025 operating cash flow of $12,330M, though equity is positive at $56,863M.

f4.evidence: Operating income rose every year from $4,571M (2020) to $8,626M (2025); operating cash flow fell from $8,856M in 2020 to $5,927M in 2022 before rising to $12,330M in 2025.

v1.evidence: Customers cannot compare - its electricity is a commodity they must buy from it, and its J.D. Power satisfaction scores are mostly at or below peer averages.

v2.evidence: Fortune ranked it No. 3 of 15 utilities in the 2026 World's Most Admired Companies (ninth straight year on the list), but it is not on major best-employer lists dominated by tech companies.

c5.evidence: If it vanished overnight, homes, hospitals and businesses across the Carolinas, Florida, Indiana, Ohio and Kentucky would lose power and gas immediately; its electricity is essential, even if not loved.
